questions.q: A transaction reads a row twice and sees different committed values each time. Which anomaly is this?
options: Non-repeatable read
Dirty read
Phantom read
Lost update

questions.q: What does MVCC fundamentally allow?
options: Writers to skip WAL logging for versioned rows entirely
Automatic escalation from row locks to table locks
Readers to see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers
Transactions to commit out of submission order safely

questions.q: Optimistic concurrency control fits best when...
options: many writers hammer the same hot row constantly all day
every worker competes to claim the same queue head row
bulk loads need exclusive table access anyway
conflicts are rare, so most transactions commit without retries

questions.q: Transaction B reads a value written by uncommitted transaction A; A then rolls back. B experienced a...
options: phantom read
dirty read
lost update
write skew anomaly

questions.q: What is the classic condition that produces a deadlock between two transactions?
options: Both hold shared locks on one row simultaneously
One transaction exceeds the configured lock wait timeout limit and gets rolled back
Each holds a lock the other needs, acquired in opposite order
Both attempt to write the same index page concurrently

questions.q: What does SELECT ... FOR UPDATE do?
options: Locks the returned rows so concurrent writers block until commit
Copies the rows into a temporary editing table for safety
Silently upgrades the transaction to serializable isolation
Prevents other transactions from even reading those rows

questions.q: In two-phase commit, what does the coordinator's first phase do?
options: Applies all writes on every participant immediately
Asks participants to prepare and durably vote yes or no
Elects a standby backup coordinator from among the voting participants
Acquires a global read lock across all involved shards

questions.q: Per the SQL standard, which isolation level still permits phantom reads?
options: Serializable isolation
Snapshot isolation as implemented in Postgres
No level does; phantoms are always blocked
Repeatable read

questions.q: Two doctors each verify 'someone else is on call', then both remove themselves; both commit under snapshot isolation. This anomaly is...
options: a dirty write
a non-repeatable read
a phantom read
write skew

questions.q: Code reads a balance, computes, then writes the result back. Concurrent runs lose an update under READ COMMITTED. Best fix?
options: Raise the isolation level to repeatable read for the initial read statement only
Use atomic updates (balance = balance - x) or SELECT FOR UPDATE
Add a covering index so the read is always current
Retry the read until two consecutive values match exactly

questions.q: How do databases typically resolve a detected deadlock?
options: Abort one victim so the rest proceed; the application retries it
Suspend both competing transactions until the lock wait timeout fully elapses
Merge the conflicting write sets into a single commit
Escalate both to table locks, forcing serial execution

questions.q: An optimistic-lock update fails its version check. What should the application do?
options: Increment the version column manually and force the write through anyway
Retry the exact same UPDATE immediately without re-reading
Re-read the row, reapply the change, then retry or surface a conflict
Wait for the competing transaction's row lock to release

questions.q: Physically, what does an UPDATE do in Postgres under MVCC?
options: Overwrites the row in place, saving the old image to an undo log
Writes a new row version; vacuum later reclaims the old one
Moves the row into a dedicated undo tablespace
Latches the page and rewrites it synchronously to disk

questions.q: Why do long-running read-only transactions still hurt an MVCC database?
options: Their shared row locks block every concurrent writer's progress until they commit
Each of their reads forces a WAL flush for consistency
They pin the query plan cache, evicting hotter plans
Old row versions must be kept for their snapshot, bloating storage

questions.q: Debit a row on shard 1 and credit a row on shard 2 atomically via 2PC. Why is this operationally painful?
options: 2PC cannot span more than two participant nodes at once
Participants deadlock against themselves during the prepare phase
A crashed coordinator leaves participants blocked, holding locks until recovery
The prepare round merely doubles commit latency and nothing else changes

questions.q: How does Postgres SERIALIZABLE (SSI) differ from classic two-phase locking?
options: It tracks read-write dependencies and aborts risky transactions instead of blocking
It takes coarser table-level locks up front to be safe
It funnels all serializable transactions through one queue
It blocks every reader until all concurrent writers commit

questions.q: A 1-second ALTER TABLE (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) queues behind a long-running query. What happens to new short SELECTs meanwhile?
options: They proceed normally, since readers never wait behind merely pending locks
They fail instantly with lock-not-available errors by default
They queue behind the waiting exclusive lock, stalling all table access
They deadlock with the ALTER and one side gets killed

questions.q: Why must a serialization-failure retry rerun the entire transaction, not just the failed statement?
options: Earlier statements read a snapshot now known to be inconsistent
The database automatically replays the earlier statements for you first
Locks from the earlier statements persist until the retry finishes
Only the final statement was rolled back by the abort

questions.q: Service X locks rows in ascending account_id order; service Y locks in arbitrary order. Deadlocks occur. Cheapest robust fix?
options: Serialize all writes through a single worker thread
Add NOWAIT to every lock acquisition and retry each failure in a loop
Shorten the database's deadlock detection interval significantly
Make Y acquire its row locks in the same sorted order as X

questions.q: Under InnoDB REPEATABLE READ, a ranged UPDATE blocks new inserts into that range. Which mechanism causes this?
options: Predicate locking that is normally available only at the serializable level
Next-key locks covering the index gaps in the scanned range
MVCC snapshot advancement pausing during the update
Page-level latch escalation on the clustered index
